comparison: Current final manuscript versus arXiv:2512.15383v1, December 17, 2025
counting_unit: Study with a distinct experimental question; parameter sweeps and extra views are not additional studies.
shared_data_note: E11 and E12 share the same 200-split cohort per dataset; E01 and E04 use views from the same dependent-Gaussian experiment family. The count is not a count of independently generated datasets.

additional_reanalysis.reason: New visualization of existing real-data timing records.

not_counted: Original independent Gaussian, distribution-table, heavy-tail, oracle/enclosure and dimension-scaling studies.
Small-calibration and additional heavy-tail stress studies omitted from the author's final selection.
Coordinate panels and bars already belonging to E01, E02, E03, or E11.

studies.name: Dependent heterogeneous Gaussian noise
studies.why: Tests whether coordinate adaptation remains useful when outputs are correlated.
studies.finding: Joint coverage, volume, runtime, and coordinate lengths distinguish scale adaptation from the smaller but under-covering copula regions.

studies.name: Partial heteroskedasticity
studies.why: Makes only five of ten coordinates input-dependent while preserving marginal second moments.
studies.finding: Separates heteroskedasticity from unequal marginal scales and assesses joint, not input-conditional, coverage.

studies.name: CQR with native CQHR
studies.why: Tests quantile-regression residuals and adds the requested CQHR baseline.
studies.finding: Outcome-space volumes and lengths show design-dependent gains of capped TSCP while identifying its inability to shrink the fitted base interval.

studies.name: Dependence-strength sweep
studies.why: Separates sensitivity to correlation from the single dependent setting in the body.
studies.finding: Varying correlation at fixed marginal scales shows stable TSCP coverage and decreasing volume as dependence strengthens.

studies.name: Coordinate-heterogeneity sweep
studies.why: Identifies when coordinate rescaling is useful by varying the largest-to-smallest noise-scale ratio.
studies.finding: The common unscaled threshold becomes less efficient as heterogeneity increases, while remaining competitive at equal scales.

studies.name: Target-coverage sweep
studies.why: Checks that the comparison is not specific to a 90 percent target.
studies.finding: Targets of 80, 90, and 95 percent show the coverage-volume trade-off and the relative behavior of the methods.

studies.name: Exchangeable contamination
studies.why: Tests the sensitivity of mean and standard deviation scaling to outliers.
studies.finding: Increasing row-wise contamination shows that near-nominal coverage can coexist with severe volume inflation.

studies.name: CQR base-interval sensitivity
studies.why: Checks dependence on the width of the fitted starting interval.
studies.finding: The base-miscoverage sweep reveals CQHR's sensitivity to fitted widths and puts the main CQR comparison in context.

studies.name: Shifted CQR scores
studies.why: Examines additive shifts as an alternative to capping signed scores.
studies.finding: Constants 100, 300, and 1000 give nearly identical recorded rectangles, equal to shifted TSCP-GWC within each run; this is not a general invariance theorem.

studies.name: Rectangular shape-template baseline
studies.why: Adds the requested comparison with the Tumu et al. family.
studies.finding: The two-dimensional KDE/mean-shift study compares coverage, normalized volume, and runtime for a specific rectangular template implementation, not every multimodal design.

studies.name: Real-data coordinate diagnostics
studies.why: Goes beyond the original two-point energy illustration with all 51 target coordinates.
studies.finding: Paired length ratios and marginal coverages show where volume gains do and do not shorten individual intervals, including unfavorable student-data results.

studies.name: Real-data search and fallback diagnostics
studies.why: Measures actual branch use, inspected candidates, and construction times.
studies.finding: No backward search or fallback occurs at miscoverage 0.1 in the tested splits; larger miscoverage levels exercise both branches without demonstrating a worst-case scan.
